questions.q: When you run the exact Lesson 26 Grover circuit for 1000 shots, what result should you expect, and why?
options: Roughly 500 shots of `11` and 500 spread across other outcomes, because Grover is probabilistic
All 1000 shots as `11`, because this N=4, M=1 case gives an exact, deterministic probability of 1.0 after one iteration
Exactly 250 shots per outcome, same as the initial uniform superposition
An error, because Grover circuits cannot be simulated
questions.explain: The N=4, M=1 case with exactly one Grover iteration is the exact special case verified in Lesson 26: probability 1.0 on |11> and 0 on every other outcome, so every one of the 1000 shots should come back as 11.

questions.q: If your simulated Grover run in Part 1 returns any outcome other than `11`, what should you check first?
options: Assume the math in Lesson 26 was wrong
Double-check the oracle (`cz(0,1)`) and the five-gate diffuser block against the original circuit for an alteration
Assume the simulator is broken and switch to real hardware
Increase the number of shots to fix it
questions.explain: Since the exact result for this specific circuit is deterministic probability 1.0, any deviation points to an error in how the oracle or diffuser gates were entered, not a flaw in the underlying verified math.

questions.q: In Part 2, when you hand-evaluate <H>(theta) = 0.5*cos(theta) + 0.3*sin(theta) at a new theta value, what information does that single evaluation give you?
options: The full shape of the curve for all theta
The derivative of <H> at that theta
Only the numeric value of <H> at that one specific theta, with no slope or derivative information
The exact location of the global minimum directly
questions.explain: A point evaluation gives you only the function's value at that one input. It tells you nothing directly about the slope there, which is exactly the constraint a gradient-free optimizer like COBYLA operates under.

questions.q: Why does this lab deliberately avoid computing or estimating a derivative of <H>(theta)?
options: Because derivatives are undefined for trigonometric functions
Because on real hardware, every <H> measurement costs real quantum shots, and estimating a derivative would require additional nearby measurements for every optimizer step
Because COBYLA requires derivatives and this lab is testing a different optimizer
Because the toy Hamiltonian has no real derivative
questions.explain: Each quantum measurement has a real cost in shots and queue time. Numerically estimating a gradient would mean paying for extra nearby measurements at every optimizer step, which is why gradient-free, point-evaluation-only optimizers like COBYLA are commonly preferred for real-hardware VQE.

questions.q: What is the true minimum value of <H>(theta) = 0.5*cos(theta) + 0.3*sin(theta), as verified in Lesson 28 and used as the target in this lab?
options: -0.5, at theta = pi
-0.583095, at theta approximately 3.6826 rad
0, at theta = pi/2
questions.explain: The verified true minimum, matching the closed form -root(0.5^2 + 0.3^2), is -0.583095 at theta approximately 3.6826 rad (about 210.96 degrees) — the target this lab's point-evaluation exercise is feeling its way toward.
